summary: Volume is the amount of space a 3D solid takes up, measured by packing it with unit cubes (side 1 unit = one cubic unit of volume); a solid packed with n unit cubes without gaps or overlaps has volume n cubic units. The core difficulty is spatial structuring — organising cubes into rows, columns and layers and accounting for HIDDEN interior cubes you cannot see from any face — not merely recalling a formula or confusing volume with surface area. Learners should distinguish volume (cubes filling space, cubic units) from area/surface area (squares covering a surface, square units).
misconceptions: Confuses volume with area or surface area (counts faces or squares rather than the space filled).
Counts only the visible/outside cubes and misses hidden interior cubes (Battista & Clements Strategy C).
Double-counts cubes along shared edges and triple-counts corners when reading a 3D drawing.

activities.title: Predict, then unpack: how many cubes fill the block?
steps: Look at a solid built from unit cubes — e.g. a 3×3×3 block shown so only three faces are visible — and PREDICT how many unit cubes make it up, stating your reasoning before building or unpacking.
Build the solid from real unit cubes (or take an existing one apart), peeling off one layer at a time to expose the middle.
Count by structuring: find how many cubes are in one layer (a 3×3 layer = 9), then how many layers (3), reaching 3 layers of 9 = 27.
Identify any cube touched by no outside face — the one hidden dead-centre — and say where it is and how many such hidden cubes there are.
Compare your first prediction with the unpacked total, and explain what you missed if they differ.
activities.insight: Volume counts EVERY cube that fills the solid, including cubes hidden at the back and buried in the interior — not just the cubes whose faces you can see. Organising the count into iterable layers lets you neither miss nor double-count cubes.

activities.title: Explore occlusion with a rotatable, sliceable solid
steps: Rotate a solid built from unit cubes to see it from every side, noticing that cubes hidden behind others from one angle become visible from another.
Peel the solid into layers and toggle transparency on the outer shell to reveal and count the interior cubes that no face shows.
Use a predict-then-reveal counter: log your first visible-only guess, then reveal the true total and compare.
Toggle an overlay of the outside squares to contrast the surface (counted in squares = area) with the cubes that fill the solid (counted in cubes = volume).
activities.insight: Rotating and slicing a 3D solid makes occlusion concrete: the cubes you could not see are really there and must be counted. Volume (filling, cubes) and surface area (covering, squares) measure different things.

activities.title: Build and fill with an isometric builder
steps: Build or fill an isometric solid by placing unit cubes, watching a live count update as you add each cube.
Use a layer tool to group the cubes into rows, columns and layers, then read off how many layers of how many cubes.

State the total as a structured product (layers × cubes-per-layer) when every layer is identical, as in a rectangular box; if layers differ, add the layer counts. Either way, use layers rather than a one-by-one tally.
activities.insight: Even in a flat isometric view, structuring the solid into layers and iterating the layer count is the reliable way to find volume and avoid miscounting.

activities.title: Count, explain and diagnose the reasoning
steps: Given an isometric drawing of a 3×3×3 cube (only three faces visible) and a pile of real unit cubes, predict the total and explain WHY before building.

Answer probe questions: Is there a cube you cannot see from any side — how many and where? If I asked for the AREA of the outside instead, would you count the same things — what is different? How can you organise your count into layers so you neither miss nor double-count a cube?
Diagnose a peer: 'A friend counted 54 by counting squares on the faces — what did they measure instead of volume?'
activities.insight: A correct volume answer pairs the total (27 cubic units) with a reason that accounts for hidden/interior cubes and distinguishes volume from surface area — the reasoning, not just the number, shows the conception.

checkQuestion: Show an isometric drawing of a cube built from unit cubes, 3 cubes along each edge (a 3×3×3), so only three faces are visible. Ask: 'How many unit cubes make up this solid, and how do you know you have counted the ones you cannot see?' Then ask: 'Is the volume the same as the area of its outside surface — why or why not?'
checkAnswer: 27 cubic units — three layers of 9 (a 3×3 layer repeated 3 times), which includes the cubes hidden at the back and the one completely inside; volume is the space filled (cubes), not the surface area (the squares on the outside).
